After an acquisition of control, the SR&ED pool is reduced to nil unless the business continues, and unused ITCs only offset tax on income from the same or similar business.

Canada's research and development tax incentive framework—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and complemented by ten provincial and territorial regimes—has undergone its most consequential legislative and administrative transformation in over a decade between December 2024 and November 2026. Enacted through Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and Federal Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025), the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, providing up to three years of upfront technical certainty within eight weeks for eligible businesses with gross business income under $25,000,000, while Federal Budget 2026 proposed a $930,000,000 five-year expansion to integrate pre-commercialisation regulatory certification and intellectual property (IP) protection expenses into the SR&ED regime. At the provincial level, Québec abolished seven legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified, fully refundable 30%/20% Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), while British Columbia expressly aligned its permanent 10% credit with the federal $6,000,000 cap and capital expenditure restoration in February 2026.
1. Legislative Chronology and Policy Evolution (2014–2026)
1.1 The Post-2012 Baseline Regime (2014–2024)

Following the enactment of the 2012 Federal Budget implementation legislation on December 14, 2012, Canada operated under a restricted SR&ED expenditure base that took full effect on January 1, 2014. Under that decade-long baseline regime, capital expenditures (formerly eligible under paragraph 37(1)(b) of the ITA) and expenditures for the right to use or lease capital property acquired or incurred after December 31, 2013, were completely excluded from both the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. In parallel, the notional overhead rate for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method (subsection 2900(4) of the ITR) was stepped down from 65% (for 2012 and prior years) to 60% in 2013, and to 55% of the eligible salary base effective January 1, 2014. Effective after 2012, only 80% of arm's length SR&ED contract payments and eligible third-party payments qualified for the ITC, introducing a 20% statutory reduction designed to exclude assumed contractor profit margins. Furthermore, effective after 2013, the basic SR&ED ITC rate decreased from 20% to 15%, while the enhanced rate for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) remained at 35% up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, phasing out where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada was between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000.
1.2 The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024)

On December 16, 2024, Government House Leader Karina Gould tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), announcing a proposed $1,900,000,000 six-year reinvestment to modernise the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. FES 2024 initially proposed four structural reforms, which were subsequently published in draft legislative proposals by the Department of Finance Canada on August 15, 2025. First, FES 2024 proposed raising the annual expenditure limit on which CCPCs earn the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, which would have yielded a maximum annual refundable credit of $1,575,000. Second, it proposed expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for determining the expenditure limit from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. Third, it proposed extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to "eligible Canadian public corporations" (ECPCs) up to the expenditure limit, subject to a straight-line phase-out based on three-year average consolidated gross revenue between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, while permitting CCPCs to elect into this gross revenue test. Fourth, it proposed reinstating the pre-2014 eligibility rules for capital expenditures (depreciable property) acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and equipment lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, for both the section 37 income deduction pool and section 127 ITC calculations.
1.3 Federal Budget 2025 and Enactment of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026)

Although the prorogation of Parliament in early 2025 temporarily delayed the FES 2024 legislative package, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne tabled Budget 2025 (Canada Strong) on November 4, 2025. Budget 2025 ratified all FES 2024 SR&ED proposals retroactive to December 16, 2024, and introduced a further expansion: increasing the annual enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit not merely to $4,500,000, but to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

The implementing legislation, Bill C-15, was enacted by Parliament and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. With Royal Assent granted, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (providing up to $2,100,000 per year in 100% refundable enhanced ITCs on current expenditures), the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out boundaries, ECPC eligibility, and capital and lease expenditure restoration are statutory law in force across Canada. In addition, pursuant to Budget 2025, the CRA officially launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026.
1.4 Federal Budget 2026: Commercialisation and IP Protection Expansion

In Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny), the federal government proposed a further structural expansion of the SR&ED program committing $930,000,000 over five years, with $235,000,000 ongoing, applicable to expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026 (November 5, 2026). While leaving credit rates, refundability percentages, and ownership rules intact, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED expenditures to encompass two categories of commercialisation expenses directly tied to an eligible SR&ED project.

The first proposed commercialisation category would cover regulatory approvals and certifications, specifically tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification required to commercialise a product or process developed through an eligible SR&ED project. The second category would cover intellectual property (IP) protection costs, specifically expenditures incurred for the registration and maintenance of IP protection (such as patents) for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Under the territoriality rules proposed in Budget 2026, administrative fees payable to a foreign IP office outside Canada would be eligible, whereas costs for supporting professional activities (such as drafting and preparing an IP application) would qualify only if conducted within Canada. If a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was claimed for IP protection costs, proposed recapture rules would apply to recover both the related SR&ED deduction and the ITC amounts. Budget 2026 also indicated that the CRA will publish sector-specific administrative guidance clarifying commercialisation expense eligibility.
2. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Regime

The federal SR&ED program is governed by three primary pillars of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.))—subsection 248(1) (definitions), section 37 (pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures), and sections 127 and 127.1 (investment tax credits and refundability)—supplemented by Part XXIX (sections 2900, 2902, and 2903) and Part XI (section 1102) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945).

body.text: 2.1 Mechanics of the Section 37(1) Deductible SR&ED Pool

Subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a cumulative, running account—the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures—calculated annually in Part 3, Section C of Form T661. Unlike ordinary business expenses deducted under section 9(1) or capital property depreciated under paragraph 20(1)(a), expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to shelter business income in any subsequent taxation year. So long as the underlying expenditures were properly reported on a timely filed Form T661 in the year they were incurred, the subsequent deduction of an accumulated pool balance is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline.

If pool reductions (such as government assistance received under paragraph 37(1)(d) or prior-year ITCs applied or refunded under paragraph 37(1)(e)) exceed the opening pool balance plus current-year additions, the resulting negative pool balance at year-end must be included in the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA. That exact income inclusion is then added back to the pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1), resetting the opening pool balance to nil (zero).

Two strict entity-level restrictions govern the section 37(1) pool. First, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) of the ITA, because a partnership is a flow-through calculation vehicle rather than a distinct taxable person, a partnership is legally barred from carrying forward any balance in its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period. The entire available pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal year must be fully deducted in computing the partnership's net income or loss for that year before allocating shares of income or loss to the partners. Second, under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) of the ITA, when a corporate claimant undergoes a loss restriction event (an acquisition of de jure control by a person or group of persons), or a trust experiences a change in its majority-interest beneficiary, the claimant's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is deemed reduced to nil at that time unless the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit. Even where that business continues, carryforward deductions from the pre-acquisition pool are strictly streamed and may only be claimed to the extent of the corporation's income for the taxation year from that same business or a similar business.
3. Scientific and Technological Eligibility: Subsection 248(1) and the "Why" and "How" Framework
3.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1) ITA)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act—a definition left unaltered by Bill C-15—"scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories. Basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as investigating the fundamental molecular characteristics of a newly discovered virus or nanomaterial to expand the scientific knowledge base. Applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, such as researching immunological mechanisms to formulate a vaccine targeting that virus's specific surface proteins. Experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c)—which accounts for the vast majority of Canadian industrial SR&ED claims—comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto, such as resolving process scale-up and thermal stability uncertainties to manufacture a vaccine or semiconductor component at industrial tolerances.
3.2 Evolution of CRA Guidance: From the Five Questions to the Two Requirements ("Why" and "How")

Historically, in its 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (derived from the Tax Court of Canada's landmark ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen), the CRA evaluated projects using a five-question administrative test:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA archived the 2015 policy document and replaced the five-question administrative checklist with the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, which consolidate the statutory elements of subsection 248(1) into Two Core Requirements: the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement. Crucially, the CRA confirms that both the archived five questions and the current two requirements derive from the identical statutory text of subsection 248(1), and the Tax Court of Canada continues to apply the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1).
Requirement 1: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

To satisfy the "Why" requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The core objective must be to generate or discover new conceptual knowledge (such as causal principles, predictive models, or technological know-how) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely collecting factual measurements or achieving commercial product functionality. New knowledge is only required when a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning it is unknown or unpredictable whether a given objective or result can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to a limitation or insufficiency in the existing scientific or technological knowledge base. The relevant baseline is the combination of publicly available scientific and technological knowledge and the existing knowledge resources accessible to the claimant's business.

If an obstacle can be resolved through routine engineering, standard procedures, or applying established methodologies known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Furthermore, the CRA explicitly specifies that if a team encounters a technical uncertainty and circumvents it using an established workaround based on available knowledge rather than investigating and resolving the underlying uncertainty, the workaround is ineligible. Whether a project ultimately succeeds or fails in achieving its target specifications does not affect SR&ED eligibility; demonstrating through systematic experimentation that a hypothesized technological approach cannot work eliminates a pathway and generates valid negative technological knowledge.

In its Guidelines on the eligibility of work, the CRA identifies eight objective indicators suggesting that existing technological knowledge available to the business is insufficient and that experimental development is required:

items: Existing design methods are not applicable to the problem.
Performance requirements or specifications do not conform to existing industry standards.
Too many interacting variables or unknowns prevent predictable modelling.
Operating parameters or environmental conditions lie outside normal operating ranges.
The technical nature of the problem is dynamically evolving.
Essential behaviour data is not readily available.
Interlocking technical constraints exist, where improving one parameter degrades another (such as latency versus cryptographic security or structural strength versus weight).

Attempting to meet reasonable cost targets imposes genuine technological uncertainty, such as re-engineering a system architecture using fundamentally different physical principles or materials (though merely substituting cheaper commercial off-the-shelf components via routine engineering does not qualify, as held in Joel Theatrical Rigging).

body.text: Requirement 2: The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

To satisfy the "How" requirement, the work must be carried out as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Merely working systematically, following project management frameworks (such as Agile sprints), or executing standard test protocols does not constitute a systematic investigation. A qualifying investigation must encompass four sequential, documented stages:

items: Defining the Problem and Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating a specific technical idea, proposed method, or causal proposition consistent with known scientific or engineering facts that serves as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the identified technological uncertainty.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Designing and executing controlled experiments, physical prototypes, simulations, or mathematical and algorithmic analyses specifically structured to test the hypothesis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively as test data is observed.

Developing Logical Conclusions: Analysing the experimental or analytical results to evaluate whether the hypothesis was validated, refuted, or requires modification, and formulating causal conclusions regarding the underlying science or technology.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Recording the hypotheses, experimental configurations, test results, and conclusions as the work progresses.

body.text: 3.3 Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA) and Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k) ITA)

Work that does not independently constitute basic research, applied research, or experimental development is eligible under paragraph 248(1)(d) if and only if it falls within one of eight exhaustive statutory categories and is both (i) commensurate with the needs (proportionate in amount, size, extent, and duration) and (ii) directly in support of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada. Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) statutorily exclude seven categories of commercial and routine work.

Not SR&ED on its own; qualifies only when directly supporting and commensurate with the needs of para. (a), (b), or (c) work in Canada. Purpose decides eligibility: data collection or testing conducted specifically to validate an experimental SR&ED hypothesis is eligible under para. (d), whereas data collection or testing for normal operations is excluded under paras. (f) and (k).
Consumer surveys, user acceptance testing for market appeal, beta demonstrations for sales prospects, and competitive feature benchmarking are strictly excluded.
Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes

Standard QA regression testing, production line inspection, and calibration against established standards are excluded. (Note: Budget 2026 proposes adding initial regulatory certification testing under commercialisation rules, and Québec's CRIC covers initial certification quality control systems).
Research in the social sciences or the humanities
Economic, sociological, linguistic, behavioural, or artistic research is excluded. Only psychological research directly supporting para. (a)–(c) science/technology work qualifies under para. (d).
Prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas

Geological exploration and resource extraction are governed by Canadian Exploration Expense (CEE) and Canadian Development Expense (CDE) regimes (ITA ss. 66–66.8), not SR&ED. Developing novel extraction machinery or metallurgical processes can still qualify if para. (c) tests are met.
Commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or commercial use of a new or improved process

Full-scale commercial manufacturing and post-deployment production operations are excluded. Where experimental development occurs simultaneously during a production run (SR&ED During Production Runs Policy), only the incremental experimental development and directly consumed/transformed experimental materials qualify.

Cosmetic, aesthetic, or ergonomic alterations that do not resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty are excluded federally. (Note: Québec's CRIC separately covers product form and aesthetics under its provincial pre-commercialization component).
Gathering operational telemetry, standard logging, or dataset scraping without supporting an active scientific/technological investigation is excluded.
Training, on-the-job learning, hiring experts to apply existing know-how, or buying proprietary knowledge

Acquiring knowledge that already exists in the industry or vendor documentation does not advance the technological knowledge base and cannot be claimed as SR&ED work. (Specific technological training in Canada for current SR&ED staff may only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method).

body.text: 4. Federal ITC Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Mechanics, Refundability, and Carryovers
4.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates and the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit

Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, the federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier rate structure applied to a claimant's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" (net of government and non-government assistance, contract payments, and provincial super-allowance benefit amounts). The Basic ITC Rate of 15% is available by default to all claimants—including corporations (foreign-controlled subsidiaries, large public corporations, and CCPCs or ECPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts.

The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35% consists of the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus an additional 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1). For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) (as defined in subsection 125(7) ITA) on up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating up to $1,050,000 in enhanced ITCs. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, under Bill C-15, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate applies to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000, generating up to $2,100,000 in enhanced ITCs.
4.2 Statutory Definition of an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)

Enacted under subsection 127(9) of the ITA by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a corporation (or a corporate subsidiary within a public group) that satisfies three cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year:

items: Canadian Residency: The corporation is resident in Canada throughout the taxation year.

Public Listing or Designation: The corporation has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or internationally (or has elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation under subsection 89(1) ITA).

Absence of Non-Resident Control: The corporation is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) ITA), by one or more non-resident persons. Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinational parent corporations remain ineligible for ECPC or CCPC status and continue to earn only the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.

body.text: 4.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out ("Grind") Formulas

The annual expenditure limit ($3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) must be shared among all associated CCPCs (under subsection 127(10.2) and Schedule T2SCH49) or among all members of a consolidated ECPC corporate group (under subsection 127(10.6)). Furthermore, the expenditure limit is subject to a straight-line reduction ("grind") based on corporate size.
A. Tax Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024 (CCPCs Only — Taxable Capital Method)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit was phased out based on the combined taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 / section 181.2 of the ITA and reported on Schedule T2SCH33) of the CCPC and all associated corporations in the immediately preceding taxation year between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 (a $40,000,000 phase-out band, reducing the limit by $0.075 for every $1 of taxable capital above $10,000,000):

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is less than or equal to $10,000,000, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital amount exceeds $10,000,000.

(Note: While a prior-year taxable income phase-out for the federal expenditure limit itself was repealed by Budget 2019 for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019, a prior-year taxable income test was retained federally solely for the "Qualifying Income Limit" used to determine 40% refundability on the 15% basic credit above the expenditure limit, as detailed in Section 4.4 below, and Ontario still retains the $500,000–$800,000 taxable income phase-out for the provincial OITC).
B. Tax Years Beginning After December 15, 2024 (CCPC Default — Taxable Capital Method)

Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada in the preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil (zero) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000. Across this $60,000,000 phase-out band ($75,000,000 minus $15,000,000), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases on a straight-line basis by $0.10 for every $1 of taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000 (whereas under the initial FES 2024 $4,500,000 proposal over the same $60,000,000 band, the reduction rate was $0.075 per $1):

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital amount is less than or equal to $15,000,000, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital amount exceeds $15,000,000.
C. Tax Years Beginning After December 15, 2024 (ECPC Mandatory & CCPC Elective — 3-Year Average Gross Revenue Method)

Because public corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital on public markets before generating commercial revenue, applying a balance-sheet taxable capital test would prematurely disqualify capital-intensive public biotech, cleantech, and deep-tech firms. Consequently, for ECPCs, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000 or greater:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if the average annual gross revenue amount is less than or equal to $15,000,000, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average annual gross revenue amount exceeds $15,000,000.

Under subsection 127(10.32) of the ITA, a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs) may elect to calculate its expenditure limit using this three-year average gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method, allowing high-capital, pre-revenue or low-revenue private corporations to preserve their full $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

Several specific administrative rules govern the revenue method and short taxation years. If an ECPC is a member of a corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), the expenditure limit is shared among all members of the consolidated group, and gross revenue is taken from the consolidated financial statements presented to shareholders at the highest level of consolidation for the preceding three fiscal years. If an entity joins or leaves the consolidated group during the year, the consolidated group's reported revenue for the year in question governs. Where a CCPC belongs to an associated group and wishes to use the revenue method under subsection 127(10.32), all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly elect on the prescribed form to use the revenue method and allocate the resulting limit among group members under subsection 127(10.6). Group revenue for associated CCPCs is computed by summing the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each group member for the preceding three fiscal years (regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire three-year period), adding each corporation's reasonable share of annual revenue from any partnership or trust in which it held an interest, and making reasonable adjustments to eliminate intra-group sales of goods or services so the group is measured as a single economic entity. If an ECPC or electing CCPC has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, average annual revenue is calculated across the actual number of completed fiscal years. Finally, under subsection 127(10.5) of the ITA, if a taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks, the corporation's expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365; where an associated CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year, the expenditure limit for a subsequent taxation year in that calendar year equals the limit determined for the first taxation year ending in that calendar year, prorated by days if the subsequent year is fewer than 51 weeks.
4.4 Refundable Investment Tax Credit Rules (Section 127.1 ITA)

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, unused SR&ED ITCs earned in the current taxation year (after reducing Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5)) may be paid out as a direct cash refund depending on the legal classification of the claimant and whether the expenditure is current or capital in nature. Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded to a taxpayer is deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5), removing it from the ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward and triggering a corresponding reduction in the following year's section 37(1) deductible expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(e).
Qualifying Corporations vs. Non-Qualifying CCPCs vs. Excluded Corporations
To determine the exact refundability percentage for a CCPC, section 127.1 distinguishes among three subcategories of CCPCs alongside ECPCs:

items: Qualifying Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2) ITA): A CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable income of all associated corporations for taxation years ending in the same calendar year) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit for the year. The Qualifying Income Limit begins at $500,000 (the federal small business deduction limit) and is phased out based on prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024:Qualifying income limit = $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000]where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is ≤ $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $10,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024:Qualifying income limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000]where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average gross revenue, if elected) is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess over $15,000,000. A CCPC that is a Qualifying Corporation (and not an Excluded Corporation) receives a 100% refund on its 35% enhanced ITCs on current expenditures (and PPA) up to the expenditure limit, a 40% refund on its 35% enhanced ITCs on restored capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and a 40% refund on its 15% basic ITCs earned on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.

Non-Qualifying CCPC (Other than an Excluded Corporation): A CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit, but whose prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average revenue) remains below the $75,000,000 upper phase-out limit. Under subsection 127.1(2.01), this CCPC still receives a 100% refund on its 35% enhanced ITCs on current expenditures (and PPA) up to its available expenditure limit, and a 40% refund on its 35% enhanced ITCs on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, but receives 0% refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit.

Excluded Corporation: A CCPC that is, at any time in the year, controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by, or related to, one or more persons exempt from tax under section 149, Her Majesty in right of a province, a Canadian municipality, or any other public authority (or any combination of them). A CCPC that is a Qualifying Corporation but is an Excluded Corporation is restricted to a 40% refund across all current and capital ITCs.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Mirroring the treatment of non-qualifying CCPCs under subsection 127.1(2.01), an ECPC receives a 100% refund of the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures and the PPA up to its expenditure limit (up to $6,000,000), a 40% refund of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit, and 0% refund (non-refundable) on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the expenditure limit.

body.text: 4.5 Carryback (3 Years) and Carryforward (20 Years) Rules for Unused ITCs

Under the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is neither deducted against Part I tax payable in the current year under subsection 127(5) nor refunded in cash under section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. When carrying back an ITC to any of the 3 preceding taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable to nil, a claimant may only carry back the current-year ITC that exceeds the amount deductible in the current year; if the claimant has Part I tax payable in the current year, the ITC amount that could have been claimed to reduce current-year Part I tax to nil cannot be carried back, even if the claimant chose not to claim it in the current year. Unused ITCs carried forward to any of the 20 subsequent taxation years are strictly non-refundable in those future years, as cash refundability under section 127.1 applies exclusively in the taxation year in which the ITC is earned. Furthermore, mirroring the subsection 37(6.1) pool streaming rules, if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control may only be carried forward to offset Part I tax payable on income from the same or a similar business, and unused ITCs earned after an acquisition of control are similarly restricted from being carried back to pre-acquisition taxation years.
5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Traditional vs. Proxy Methods, and Cost Eligibility Rules
5.1 Salaries and Wages (Subsection 37(8), Subsection 78(4), and Regulation 2900)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (sections 5 to 8 of the ITA—that is, employment income subject to T4 source deductions), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances. Dividends paid to shareholder-founders are distributions of corporate after-tax profit, not employment income, and are 100% ineligible for SR&ED claims.
Directly Engaged (Proxy Method) vs. Directly Undertaking, Supervising, or Supporting (Traditional Method)

Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) ITA and Regulation 2900(5)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada can be claimed. "Directly engaged" requires hands-on technical execution of basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work. First-line technical supervisors and managers qualify only for the exact hours spent providing direct technical input or technically directing the course of ongoing experiments; non-technological management, administrative decision-making, and supervision above the first line are excluded. Clerical, administrative, human resources, accounting, legal, and purchasing staff are never considered directly engaged under the Proxy Method.

Under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) ITA and Regulation 2900(2)(b)–(c)), in addition to hands-on technical staff who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED, a claimant may claim the salary or wages of clerical and administrative staff on Line 360 (Overhead and other expenditures), provided their services are shown to be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their employment time throughout the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages qualifies. Otherwise, the salary is prorated based on contemporaneous time-tracking records, such as timesheets, Git commit logs, Jira or Linear sprint logs, and negative time reporting.
Inclusions, Exclusions, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

For non-specified employees, eligible wage components include base salary, regular wages, statutory holiday pay, regular annual vacation pay, regular sick leave pay, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, cash outlays for taxable benefits, inducement payments, and commissions incurred in the year. Conversely, four categories of compensation are statutorily excluded from SR&ED salary or wages:

items: Employer's Share of Payroll Benefits: Employer contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Québec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), Workers' Compensation Boards (WSIB/CNESST), registered pension plans, or group medical, dental, and optical insurance plans are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages. (Under the Traditional Method, employer payroll benefits for hands-on SR&ED staff may be claimed separately as overhead on Line 360; under the Proxy Method, they are covered by the 55% PPA).
Stock Option Benefits (Section 7 ITA): Stock options granted or shares issued are deemed not to be an expenditure incurred by the corporation and are strictly excluded.
Extended Vacation or Sick Leave: Leave in excess of normal annual earned entitlements is excluded because no SR&ED duties are performed during extended leave.

Retiring Allowances (Severance): Excluded from salary or wages under subsection 248(1); retiring allowances are only claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if they form part of a written pre-existing employment contract meeting the directly related and incremental tests.

body.text: Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA (the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule), any salary, wage, or bonus accrued in a taxation year that is not actually paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. It is excluded from that year's SR&ED claim and may only be claimed as a deductible SR&ED expenditure (on Form T661 Line 310) in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Crucially, however, under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year and claimed on Line 310 are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base—meaning late payment beyond 180 days permanently forfeits the 55% proxy overhead top-up on those wages.
Specified Employees: Statutory Caps and 2023–2026 YMPE Thresholds

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, parent, or child of a controlling shareholder). Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions:

items: Total Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9) ITA): Any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is 100% prohibited from being claimed as an SR&ED expenditure or included in the PPA salary base.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap of 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1) ITA): The maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed in the section 37(1) pool and for direct ITC purposes for a specified employee (after multiplying eligible base salary plus eligible taxable benefits by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year:Maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages = 5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee of the claimant.If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no SR&ED salary may be claimed at all by any of the corporations unless they file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the allocation (which cannot exceed 5 × YMPE across the entire associated group).

PPA Salary Base Cap of Lesser of 75% of Total Eligible Wages or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7) & 2900(8)): When calculating the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method, a specified employee's contribution is restricted to the lesser of: (i) the actual eligible SR&ED salary claimed (excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, and prior-year unpaid wages); (ii) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); and (iii) 2.5 × YMPE prorated by the total number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee), shared across all associated corporations under Regulation 2900(8): limb (iii) = 2.5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual.

body.text: Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) ITA)

Under subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2) of the ITA, a claimant may include a limited amount of "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work physically performed outside Canada in both its domestic section 37(1) pool and its PPA salary base, provided five strict cumulative statutory conditions are met:

items: The foreign SR&ED work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant (foreign subcontractors and consultants are 100% excluded).
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the wage expenditure was incurred.
The work relates to a business of the claimant.
The work performed outside Canada is an integral part and solely in support of an eligible SR&ED project carried on in Canada.

The salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by a foreign country. Under subsection 37(1.5), the maximum permissible foreign SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed in a taxation year is strictly capped at 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during that taxation year.

body.text: 5.2 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Prescribed Proxy Amount at 55%)

A claimant must choose annually between the Traditional Method (Form T661 Line 162) and the Proxy Method (Form T661 Line 160). Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, this election must be made when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year. If a claimant fails to make an election on Line 160, the Traditional Method applies automatically by default.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant foregoes claiming actual overhead and indirect support expenditures in the section 37(1) pool (deducting them instead as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1) of the ITA) and calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible salary base (Regulation 2900(4)). The PPA is not added to the section 37(1) deductible pool, but is added (on Line 502 of Form T661) to "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to earn federal (and certain provincial) ITCs.
The Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))
To prevent single-purpose R&D shell companies from claiming a notional 55% PPA that exceeds their actual total non-SR&ED business expenses, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA:
PPA ≤ A − (B + C)

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing the claimant's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed in the year under section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest expense, and bad debts), section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), section 26 (banks), section 30 (land improvements for farming), section 32 (insurance agents and brokers), section 37 (SR&ED pool deductions), sections 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development), and section 104 (trusts); and C is the total of all expenditures incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as office or laboratory building rent). Because building rent (C) and direct SR&ED pool deductions (B) are subtracted from total business deductions (A), a pure-play startup whose only expenses are SR&ED developer salaries and office building rent can be constrained by the Overall PPA Cap unless it has at least $55 of other non-building ordinary operating expenses (such as administrative salaries, marketing, legal and audit fees, insurance, or general cloud and IT costs) for every $100 of salary in the PPA base.
Traditional Method Overhead: The "Directly Related" and "Incremental" Dual Test (Regulation 2900(2)(c))

When a claimant uses the Traditional Method, overhead and other current expenditures claimed on Line 360 of Form T661 must satisfy two strict cumulative tests under Regulation 2900(2)(c) (or be directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment under Regulation 2900(3)). First, under the Directly Related Test, the expenditure must connect directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED, allocated using a rational, documented methodology. Second, under the Incremental Test, the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred.

Furthermore, under Regulation 2902, certain expenditures that may satisfy the directly related and incremental tests are prescribed expenditures that are excluded from "qualified expenditures" and therefore earn no ITC (including fees paid to consultants or accountants for preparing SR&ED claims, costs to attend scientific conventions or conferences, and interest or financing expenses). Similarly, under the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, recruiting expenses (headhunter fees, job advertisements, interview travel, and work permit or visa immigration fees) are treated as regular business expenses and cannot be claimed in the SR&ED pool or for ITCs, whereas moving expenses to relocate selected SR&ED candidates or employees within Canada qualify under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental.
