5.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) & Regulation 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), the cost of materials may be claimed under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (and paid within 180 days of year-end under subsection 127(26) to earn an ITC). To qualify as "materials for SR&ED," the raw materials, substances, or component parts must be physical and tangible (that is, in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible "thing" (an intermediate product, by-product, or final product) on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED.

Materials consumed are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the SR&ED experimentation (such as chemical reagents, metal stock destroyed in destructive stress testing, or cardboard substrates ruined during experimental printing trials); materials consumed do not trigger ITC recapture. Materials transformed are materials or component parts that are incorporated into a prototype, custom product, experimental production run, or commercial asset during SR&ED, and that retain commercial value or remain intact after testing. While 100% claimable in the year transformed, if the resulting prototype or product is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the cost of the transformed materials is subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36).

General laboratory supplies and consumables that do not compose the body of the experimental object—such as test tubes, pipettes, beakers, flasks, Petri dishes, filter papers, cleaning products, lubricants, solvents, CDs/DVDs, and general utilities (electricity, water, natural gas)—are not eligible as SR&ED materials. They can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method (and are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method). For valuation purposes, purchased materials are valued at laid-down cost (invoice price plus customs and excise duties, freight, and storage), whereas internally manufactured inventory items used in SR&ED include direct materials, direct labour, and a reasonable share of production overhead (even if the claimant uses the Proxy Method). Purchases from a non-arm's length supplier are restricted for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier under subsection 127(11.6), eliminating intra-group profit markups.
5.4 Audit Treatment of Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, GCP), Software Licences, and Bandwidth

A frequent point of friction in Canadian software and artificial intelligence SR&ED audits involves the classification of cloud computing infrastructure (such as Amazon Web Services [AWS], Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform [GCP]), SaaS tools, and software licences. Although several commercial advisory blogs colloquially describe segmented R&D cloud computing bills (dev, test, and staging environments or GPU training runs) as "materials consumed", the CRA's authoritative Materials for SR&ED Policy strictly requires SR&ED materials to be physical and tangible objects in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state that compose the body of a tangible thing. Because cloud computing services and SaaS subscriptions are intangible services rather than tangible matter, CRA Financial Reviewers routinely disallow cloud computing costs claimed on the "Materials" line under the Proxy Method unless they qualify as an equipment lease or capital expenditure.

With Bill C-15's restoration of equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, the CRA's updated Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) explicitly addresses remote computing and bandwidth. Relying on the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877 (TCC)—where the Court held that payments for a dedicated telecommunications line and access to a remote mainframe computer constituted a lease of tangible optoelectronic and computing equipment rather than general office overhead—the CRA allows post-December 15, 2024 costs for dedicated bandwidth and dedicated remote computing hardware (which are not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture [GPOEF]) to be claimed as a lease of equipment, even under the Proxy Method, provided the leased computing resource satisfies the ASA (≥ 90% SR&ED use → 100% claimable on Line 350) or Primarily (> 50% to < 90% SR&ED use → 50% claimable on Line 355) operating-time thresholds. For shared or on-demand cloud environments that do not constitute a lease of dedicated hardware, costs segmented strictly to SR&ED development and testing environments (excluding production hosting) are claimable as directly related and incremental overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. Conversely, physical AI and machine learning hardware (such as NVIDIA GPU clusters, local development servers, and test benches) and purchased perpetual software licences acquired after December 15, 2024, and used ≥ 90% (ASA) in SR&ED qualify directly as SR&ED capital expenditures under restored paragraph 37(1)(b) (or, if not claimed in SR&ED, under CCA Class 12 or Class 50 with the reinstated Accelerated Investment Incentive).
5.5 Subcontractors (Contract Expenditures) and Third-Party Payments
The Income Tax Act draws a sharp legal and financial distinction among (A) Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts, (B) Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts, and (C) Third-Party Payments.
A. Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) & Subsection 127(9) ITA)

When a claimant (the payer) contracts an arm's length "taxable supplier" (a Canadian-resident individual, partnership, or corporation, or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is added to the payer's section 37(1) deductible pool, but only 80% of the contract expenditure is included in the payer's "qualified expenditures" for calculating the federal ITC. In an audit, the CRA examines the Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statements of Work (SOWs) to verify that the work was performed on behalf of the payer. The payer must bear the financial risk of technological failure (such as paying on a Time & Materials basis rather than a fixed-price contract where the contractor only gets paid if a working commercial milestone is delivered) and must retain ownership of, or an exclusive right to exploit, the resulting intellectual property.

If the arm's length contractor also files its own SR&ED claim, any amount received or receivable from the payer constitutes a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18), which reduces the contractor's own qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar so only the payer claims the ITC. Furthermore, if the payer contracts out only paragraph 248(1)(d) support work (such as testing or machinist fabrication), the payer can claim the contract cost in support of its Canadian SR&ED project, whereas the contractor cannot claim support work on its own. Under the Contract Look-Through Rule (subsections 37(14) and 37(15) ITA), if a contractor incurs non-current expenditures in fulfilling an SR&ED contract, the payer's eligible contract expenditure is reduced accordingly, and the performer is statutorily required under subsection 37(15) to notify the payer in writing of the reduction amount without delay upon request, or no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year.
B. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Section 251, Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) & Subsection 127(13) ITA)

When a payer enters into an SR&ED contract with a related or non-arm's length performer (as defined in section 251 of the ITA, such as a sister corporation, parent, subsidiary, or corporation controlled by the same shareholder group), paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) provides that payments made to the non-arm's length contractor are deductible in the payer's section 37(1) pool, but are not qualified expenditures for the payer's ITC calculation (0% ITC to payer). Instead, the amount received by the NAL performer is excluded from the definition of "contract payment," allowing the NAL performer to claim the underlying SR&ED salaries, materials, and overhead on its own Form T661 and Schedule 31. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) may jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), transferring the performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the payer on Lines 508 and 510 (transferee) and Line 544 (transferor) of Form T661. Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24) of the ITA, a claimant cannot circumvent the NAL contract restrictions by routing an SR&ED contract through an arm's length intermediary that subcontracts the work back to a party not dealing at arm's length with the claimant.
C. Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) ITA & Form T1263)

Unlike an SR&ED contract (where the payer directs the work, retains exclusive IP rights, and accounts on an accrual basis), a third-party payment is a payment made to an external research entity—classified by the CRA into Categories A through F: A (Canadian-resident corporations), B (approved associations), C (approved universities, colleges, or research institutes), D (tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j)), E (approved granting councils), and F (paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit corporations conducting basic or applied research relevant to multiple businesses)—where the performer controls the research, results are generally published, multiple funders typically participate, and the claimant obtains a non-exclusive (preferential) right to exploit the results in its business. Third-party payments to Category B through F entities are claimed on a cash (paid) basis, whereas Category A corporate third-party payments are claimed in the year the SR&ED is performed. Like arm's length contracts, 80% of an eligible third-party payment qualifies for the federal ITC, and every claimant reporting a third-party payment must complete and attach prescribed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) to Form T661.
5.6 Restored Capital Expenditures and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted by Bill C-15, paragraph 37(1)(b) of the ITA and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) restore both immediate 100% income deductibility and ITC eligibility for SR&ED capital expenditures on property acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.
Qualifying Criteria for Restored Capital Expenditures (CRA Capital Expenditures Policy, Updated June 29, 2026)

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method), and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method), five statutory conditions must be satisfied:

items: Depreciable Property Ownership: The expenditure must be incurred to acquire depreciable property (as defined in subsection 13(21) ITA—property with an expected useful life exceeding 12 months for which CCA could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a)) that is owned by the claimant or in which the claimant holds a leasehold interest. Non-depreciable property (such as land, inventory, or goodwill) is strictly excluded.

All or Substantially All (ASA — ≥ 90%) Intention Test: At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either that (i) the property will be used during all or substantially all (≥ 90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or that (ii) all or substantially all (≥ 90%) of its value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada. While evaluated based on intent at acquisition, the CRA audits actual subsequent usage via equipment logbooks. (Note: The CRA's June 29, 2026 Capital Expenditures Policy notes that property used for both commercial activities and SR&ED that fails the 90% ASA threshold may instead be evaluated under the Shared-Use Equipment [SUE] rules).

New vs. Used Property Distinction: While used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that meets the 90% ASA test qualifies for the immediate section 37(1)(b) income deduction, used property is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) and does NOT qualify for SR&ED ITCs; to earn the 35% or 15% ITC, the capital property must be new (not previously used for any purpose by any person before acquisition by the claimant).

Exclusion of Buildings and GPOEF: Capital expenditures to acquire a building or a leasehold interest in a building (including laboratory or factory buildings) are strictly disallowed under paragraph 37(8)(d). Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, telephones, and cell phones, excluding computers, hardware, software, and ancillary computing equipment) is excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures and must be depreciated through standard CCA classes.

The "Available for Use" Timing Rule (Subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2) ITA): Under subsection 37(1.2) and amended subsection 127(11.2), a capital expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred or acquired for section 37 pool or section 127 ITC purposes until the depreciable property becomes "available for use" by the taxpayer (the earliest of the time it is first used in SR&ED or delivered and capable of being used) after December 15, 2024. As highlighted in technical tax commentary (Scitax Bulletin #84), if specialized R&D equipment was ordered and delivered prior to December 16, 2024, but was not installed, calibrated, and "available for use" until after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(11.2) provides a technical basis for claiming the ITC in the taxation year it became available for use.

body.text: Restored Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify as current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a)—meaning they earn 100% refundability at the 35% enhanced rate for CCPCs and ECPCs, unlike capital purchases which earn 40% refundability on the 35% credit. Where leased equipment satisfies ASA Usage (≥ 90% operating time), 100% of the lease cost is claimable on Line 350 under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method). Where leased equipment satisfies Primarily Usage (> 50% to < 90% operating time), 50% of the lease payment is claimable on Line 355 under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI) ITA, excluding GPOEF), whereas the exact proportional SR&ED usage percentage is claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. Where leased equipment is used ≤ 50% of operating time, 0% is claimable under the Proxy Method, while the proportional SR&ED percentage remains claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental. Lease payments (rent) for a building remain strictly disallowed under subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii), with the sole statutory exception of a prescribed special-purpose building approved on a building-by-building basis by the Department of Finance Canada under Regulation 2903.
5.7 The 20-Year SR&ED ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) ITA)

To ensure that SR&ED tax credits subsidize only the net cost of R&D rather than commercial assets, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA impose a 20-year recapture window (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)). Recapture is triggered whenever a claimant (or a non-arm's length transferee) disposes of, or converts to commercial use, any property—including restored SR&ED capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, or materials transformed into a prototype, custom product, or commercial asset—for which an SR&ED ITC was claimed within the preceding 20 taxation years.

In the taxation year of disposition or conversion to commercial use, the claimant must add directly to its Part I tax payable the lesser of: (1) the actual SR&ED ITC originally earned on the particular property; and (2) the historical ITC percentage rate (such as 35% or 15%) multiplied by (a) the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's length party) or (b) the fair market value (FMV) of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use or disposition to a non-arm's length party. Under subsection 127(32) of the ITA, for recapture purposes, the "cost" of a property never exceeds the amount paid to acquire the property from third parties; internal SR&ED salaries, wages, and overhead imputed to building a prototype are never subject to ITC recapture. Similarly, where IP accrues to a payer under an SR&ED contract, converting or selling that IP does not trigger subsection 127(27) recapture (though under the Budget 2026 proposals, disposing of IP for which new IP protection commercialisation costs were claimed would trigger dedicated recapture rules). Any ITC recapture amount added to Part I tax payable in a year is added back to the claimant's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2). Additionally, for capital property deducted under paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 37(6) deems the SR&ED deduction to be CCA allowed under section 13, potentially triggering standard recaptured CCA income inclusion under subsection 13(1) upon sale.
5.8 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and the Concessional Loan Fix (Bill C-69)

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA, both the deductible SR&ED pool and qualified expenditures for ITC calculations must be reduced on a project-by-project basis by the amount of any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, or provincial R&D tax credits from any federal, provincial, municipal, or foreign government or public authority, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself) or non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements within the meaning of paragraph 12(1)(x)) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the time of filing. Where assistance exceeds one group member's expenditures or applies across related corporations, it may be allocated using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20). Conversely, under paragraph 37(1)(c) and subsections 127(10.7)–(10.8) of the ITA, when a claimant repays government or non-government assistance (such as repaying a conditionally repayable contribution based on commercial revenues) that previously reduced its SR&ED pool, the repayment is added to the section 37(1) pool in the year paid and earns non-refundable ITCs (repayments of assistance do not qualify for cash refunds under section 127.1).

Following the Tax Court of Canada's controversial decision in CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178 (leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed May 25, 2023, No. 40504)—which held that an unconditionally repayable low-interest (2.5%) loan from Industry Canada's Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative was not an "ordinary commercial agreement" and therefore constituted "government assistance" that disqualified $250,000,000 of CAE's SR&ED expenditures—Parliament enacted Bill C-69 in 2024. Amending subsection 127(9), subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix), and adding subsection 12(11) of the ITA retroactive to January 1, 2020, the law now explicitly exempts an "excluded loan" from being treated as government assistance. An "excluded loan" is a non-forgivable loan, evidenced in writing, provided by a government, municipality, or other public authority in Canada (such as BDC, EDC, CIB, FCC, or regional development agencies) where, at the time the loan was granted, bona fide arrangements were made for repayment within a reasonable time and the funds are used to earn income from a business or property.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking Mechanics

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) offer statutory R&D tax credits that stack with the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories (NWT), and Nunavut—offer no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.
6.1 The Federal-Provincial Assistance Grind Mechanic

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance. Consequently, provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base before the 35% or 15% federal ITC rate is applied (whereas the federal SR&ED ITC never reduces the provincial expenditure base).

Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a claimant uses the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as Ontario's OITC or B.C.'s SR&ED credit) that is attributable to the notional 55% PPA does not reduce the section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (because the PPA itself is never in the section 37(1) pool); instead, that portion reduces federal "qualified expenditures" for ITC calculation purposes on Form T661 (Line 513) and must be included directly in taxable income on T2 Schedule 1 under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received. Furthermore, where a corporation cannot utilize a non-refundable provincial R&D credit (such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC or B.C.'s 10% non-refundable credit) because it has no provincial income tax payable, claiming the provincial credit would still trigger an immediate 35% or 15% federal ITC reduction under subsection 127(18). To prevent losing federal cash or usable federal ITCs for an unusable provincial carryforward, statutes in Ontario (Taxation Act, 2007, s. 43 [ORDTC] and s. 96(14) [OITC]), British Columbia (non-refundable credit only), Manitoba, Nova Scotia, and Saskatchewan explicitly allow a corporation to waive or renounce the provincial credit by the statutory deadline, thereby avoiding the federal assistance grind.
6.2 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Information Bulletin 2025-6)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6, confirmed by Revenu Québec on July 9, 2025), the Government of Québec executed the most sweeping restructuring of provincial innovation taxation in Canada, committing $2,400,000,000 over five years.
Elimination of Seven Legacy Québec Tax Measures (Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished seven legacy innovation tax measures (which remain claimable only for taxation years that began before March 26, 2025):

items: Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly under Taxation Act (Québec) s. 1029.7, claimed on Form RD-1029.7, which offered a 14% basic rate and up to a 30% enhanced rate for SMEs with prior-year assets below $50,000,000, phasing out to 14% at $75,000,000);
Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.6);
Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.9.03);
Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (formerly Form RD-1029.8.16.1);
Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services;
The Industrial Design Component of the Design Tax Credits (Note: the fashion design component remains in force); and
The Personal Income Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts.

body.text: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the abolished credits are replaced by the single, unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation), administered by Revenu Québec. Unlike the federal SR&ED credit or the legacy Québec R&D salary credit, the CRIC operates on a size-neutral, two-tier rate structure that is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations operating an establishment in Québec—including large corporations, public corporations, and foreign-controlled subsidiaries—regardless of asset size or revenue. Every eligible corporation earns a 30% fully refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures that exceed the corporation's applicable exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and a 20% fully refundable rate on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 threshold (with no upper expenditure cap). To claim the CRIC, a corporation's qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed an annual Applicable Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec basic personal amount under the personal income tax system (for example, $18,571 for 2025 / $18,952 for 2026) for each employee, multiplied by the percentage of time devoted by that employee to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year.

While Québec's R&D definition remains harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) (with the CRA performing the scientific review of the R&D component), the CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec as a continuation of, or in conjunction with, Québec R&D. Eligible pre-commercialization work includes: (i) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements to obtain an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (ii) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and selection of materials; and (iii) quality control activities relating strictly to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial regulatory approval or certification.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC encompass four specific cost categories: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Québec (Québec does not allow a 55% notional overhead proxy; only actual eligible costs qualify); (2) 50% of amounts paid to an arm's length subcontractor for work carried out in Québec (and 100% of direct salaries for non-arm's length Québec subcontractors); (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and (4) 100% of capital property acquisition costs for new depreciable machinery and equipment (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings) acquired for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec. If the capital property ceases to be used solely in Québec for eligible activities within 730 consecutive days (2 years) of commencement of use, the CRIC is recovered via a special recapture tax. A corporation cannot stack the CRIC on the same capital property with the Québec Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation (C3i) or a Large Investment Project tax holiday.

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec's Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) calculates its Québec nexus ratio using CRIC R&D expenditures (unreduced by the $50,000+ exclusion threshold, but excluding pre-commercialization expenditures). Similarly, on federal Form T661 (Line 429a) and Québec Form RD-222 (Line 71), only the R&D component of the CRIC reduces the federal SR&ED deductible pool and qualified expenditures as government assistance. Claimants file Form RD-222 (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures), Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization), Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (associated group expenditure limit agreement), and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (pre-commercialization information return) with their Québec CO-17 corporate income tax return within 18 months of tax year-end.
6.3 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC (Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario))

Ontario operates three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) (S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A), administered jointly with the CRA via the T2 corporate return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96 & Ontario Regulation 37/09, T2 Schedule 566, Schedule 5 Line 468) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (generating a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000), shared among associated corporations. Unlike the federal government and British Columbia, Ontario retained its $3,000,000 expenditure limit and did not increase it to $6,000,000; Ontario spending between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000 earns the 35% federal ITC and 3.5% Ontario ORDTC, but 0% OITC. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Per official Ontario Ministry of Finance guidance (updated October 30, 2026), Ontario harmonized with the federal restoration of capital property: the OITC base includes 100% of current expenditures (including the Ontario PPA) plus 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (while excluding capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45, T2 Schedule 508, Schedule 5 Line 416) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment, with no expenditure limit and no income or capital phase-out (and includes restored capital expenditures on or after December 16, 2024). Unused ORDTC may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Under Ontario law, the 8% OITC (and 20% OBRITC) constitutes government assistance for ORDTC purposes and reduces the qualified expenditure base before the 3.5% ORDTC is calculated (whereas the ORDTC does not reduce the OITC base). Both the OITC and ORDTC (unless waived in writing under s. 96(14) or s. 43) then reduce the federal SR&ED expenditure base.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — T2 Schedules 568 and 569, Schedule 5 Line 470) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified payments made under an eligible contract with an approved Ontario research institute (universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institutes), up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (yielding up to $4,000,000 in refundable credits), with a separate Schedule 569 filed for each eligible contract.
6.4 British Columbia: Express Alignment with Bill C-15 (Income Tax Act (B.C.) ss. 97–103)

Administered by the CRA on Form T666 (British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit), British Columbia provides a 10% SR&ED tax credit for corporations (including corporate partners of partnerships) with a B.C. permanent establishment. In B.C. Budget 2026 (tabled February 17, 2026), British Columbia enacted the most comprehensive provincial alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms. B.C. Budget 2026 permanently removed the statutory sunset date from the B.C. SR&ED credit, raised the annual expenditure limit for its 10% fully refundable credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (increasing the maximum annual B.C. cash refund from $300,000 to $600,000), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, as qualifying B.C. expenditures. Expenditures above the $6,000,000 limit and expenditures incurred by non-CCPC and non-ECPC corporations earn a 10% non-refundable B.C. credit, which can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years (or renounced to preserve the federal ITC base). Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of the corporation's taxation year-end.
6.5 Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — Alberta Corporate Tax Act ss. 26.95–26.99)

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta administers its own independent refundable R&D incentive—the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—through the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under Division 7 of Part 6 (sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970. The IEG operates on a two-tier incremental rate structure (8% base plus 12% incremental, for a 20% maximum refundable rate). Under the Part I Base Payment (8% Refundable), every corporation with an Alberta permanent establishment earns an 8% fully refundable credit on its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to its Base Amount (calculated on Line 118 of AT1 Schedule 29 as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures for the two immediately preceding taxation years). Under the Part II Incremental Enhancement (+12% Refundable, for a 20% Total Rate), on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures that exceed the two-year historical Base Amount, the corporation earns an additional 12% refundable credit, yielding a combined 20% fully refundable credit on incremental R&D growth (or on 100% of spending for a first-year R&D claimant whose prior two-year average is $0).

The IEG applies to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $4,000,000 (shared among associated corporations, yielding a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000), which phases out on a straight-line basis when prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (from T2 Schedule 33, Line 690) is between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. As confirmed by Alberta TRA guidance updated June 30, 2026, Alberta did not adopt the federal $6,000,000 cap or the restoration of capital expenditures. Capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024, are excluded from the IEG; on AT1 Schedule 29, corporations with taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, must pull current SR&ED expenditures from Line 557 of federal Form T661 (rather than total qualified expenditures on Line 559), while calculating the Alberta proxy amount at 55% of Alberta SR&ED salaries on Line 009. The statutory filing deadline for AT1 Schedule 29 is 15 months after the AT1 filing due date (21 months after year-end), though federal T661 verification within the 18-month federal deadline is required for disbursement.
6.6 Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

In Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) ss. 63–63.4, T2 Schedule 403), for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, the province doubled its 10% refundable expenditure threshold for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (providing up to $200,000 in refundable credits). Expenditures above $2,000,000 (and expenditures by non-CCPCs) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward), subject to a combined total annual credit cap of $1,000,000 ($10,000,000 in expenditures).

In Manitoba (The Income Tax Act (Manitoba) s. 7.3, T2 Schedule 380), the province provides a 15% credit on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures (which continuously included current expenditures and non-building depreciable capital equipment even prior to the federal restoration), with no expenditure limit. For R&D performed under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute, 100% of the credit (15%) is refundable; for in-house R&D, 50% is refundable (7.5% effective rate) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5% effective rate), with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward. Schedule 380 must be filed within 12 months after the T2 filing due date (18 months post year-end).

Across Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia) s. 41, T2 Schedule 340) provides a flat 15% fully refundable tax credit to all corporations with a Nova Scotia permanent establishment, with no expenditure cap, filed within 18 months of tax year-end. New Brunswick (New Brunswick Income Tax Act s. 59, T2 Schedule 360) provides a flat 15% fully refundable tax credit to all corporations with a New Brunswick permanent establishment, with no expenditure cap. Newfoundland and Labrador (Income Tax Act, 2000 (Newfoundland and Labrador) s. 42, T2 Schedule 301 / Form T1129) provides a flat 15% fully refundable tax credit to both corporations and individuals, filed within 12 months after the tax return filing due date, and is unique in Canada in that its statutory expenditure base is not reduced by government or non-government assistance (other than GST/HST input tax credits). Finally, Yukon (Income Tax Act (Yukon) s. 15, T2 Schedule 442 [Schedule 5 Line 698] / Form T1232) provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit to corporations and Yukon-resident individuals, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% combined) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University, filed within 18 months of the end of the taxation year.

body.text: 7. Governing Bodies, Prescribed Forms, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Procedures
7.1 Governing Authorities and Division of Responsibilities

Four key government institutions administer R&D tax incentives across Canada. The Department of Finance Canada formulates federal tax policy, drafts legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (such as Bill C-15 and Budget 2026), and approves prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits except Québec and Alberta through its Business Tax Incentives Directorate and regional Coordinating Tax Services Offices. Within the CRA, Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (reporting to Research and Technology Managers [RTMs] and supported by National Technology Sector Specialists [NTSS]) evaluate scientific and technological eligibility under subsection 248(1), while Financial Reviewers (FRs) (reporting to Financial Review Managers [FRMs]) audit expenditure allowability, proxy calculations, and ITC entitlements under sections 37, 127, and 127.1. In Québec, Revenu Québec and the Ministère des Finances du Québec administer the CRIC and legacy R&D credits under the Taxation Act (Québec); while Revenu Québec audits all financial expenditures and pre-commercialization criteria, Québec law harmonizes with the CRA's scientific review for the R&D component. In Alberta, the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, disbursing payments following CRA verification of the federal T661 claim.
7.2 Complete Catalogue of Prescribed Federal SR&ED Forms

Under subsections 37(11), 37(12), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA, SR&ED tax incentives are strictly contingent upon filing the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline:

items: Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, current version t661-26e.pdf / t661-fill-26e.pdf, accompanied by Guide T4088): Mandatory for all claimants to report technical project narratives (Part 2), calculate the section 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures (Part 3), calculate qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (Part 4), compute the PPA salary base and 55% PPA (Part 5), list project costs (Part 6), report statistical data (Part 7), disclose mandatory claim preparer and contingency-fee billing arrangements (Part 9, under subsection 37(11)(b) and subsection 162(5.1) penalty rules), and execute the non-revocable officer certification (Part 10).

Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, current version t2sch31-10-26e.pdf): Mandatory for corporate claimants to calculate, deduct, carry back, carry forward, or claim a cash refund of SR&ED ITCs, or report ITC recapture.

Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit): Mandatory to allocate the $6,000,000 ($3,000,000 pre-Dec 16, 2024) expenditure limit among associated CCPCs under subsection 127(10.2) (supplemented by a dedicated schedule released in Fall 2026 for subsection 127(10.6) allocations among consolidated ECPCs and CCPCs electing the revenue method under subsection 127(10.32)).
Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals), current version t2038-ind-25e.pdf): Mandatory for individuals and trusts to claim SR&ED ITCs.

Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length): Allocates excess government or non-government assistance among non-arm's length group members under subsection 127(20).

Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, Schedule 62, version t1146-26e.pdf): Transfers qualified SR&ED expenditures from a non-arm's length performer to a payer under subsection 127(13).

Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED): Mandatory (along with a certified directors' resolution) when a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations.
Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED): Mandatory schedule for each third-party payment claimed under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), or (iii).

Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval): Prescribed application form for the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process launched April 1, 2026.
Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) & Form T400A / RC592 (Notice of Objection): Prescribed recourse and dispute forms.

body.text: 7.3 The Strict 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Consequences of Deficiencies

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For corporations (T2), the T2 filing due date is 6 months after the taxation year-end; adding 12 months yields a strict SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For individuals carrying on a business (T1), the T1 filing due date is June 15 of the following calendar year; adding 12 months yields a reporting deadline of June 15 of the second following calendar year (17.5 months after a December 31 year-end). For trusts (T3), the T3 filing due date is 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end; adding 12 months yields a reporting deadline of 15 months (90 days plus 12 months) after the trust's taxation year-end. Where a partnership files a T5013 Partnership Information Return, Form T661 must be filed with the T5013 no later than 12 months after the earliest filing due date of any member for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends, and individual or corporate partners must file their respective Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND) by their own SR&ED reporting deadlines.

Under subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA, the Minister of National Revenue has zero statutory discretion to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline or waive the prescribed form requirement under subsection 220(2.1). Because the CRA requires at least 90 days to conduct a completeness screening, the CRA officially recommends filing the complete SR&ED claim simultaneously with the tax return (at 6 months post year-end) or at least 90 days prior to the 18-month deadline.

body.text: 7.4 The CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Effective April 1, 2026 (announced April 8, 2026), the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, enabling eligible businesses to obtain binding upfront technical confirmation that their planned R&D projects meet the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED before commencing work or incurring major costs (or shortly after starting work). To qualify, the applicant must be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or Canadian partnership, have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA. Each application can cover up to 3 projects, provided the projects have not been included in a previous SR&ED claim and do not involve issues currently under litigation. Pre-claim approval evaluates technical project eligibility only; it does not audit expenditures upfront.
The application follows a structured four-step workflow:

items: Step 1 — Request a Case Number: Submit the online CRA web form (taking under 5 minutes). Existing claimants in good standing receive a case number within 2 business days via My Business Account; all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by telephone.

Step 2 — Complete and Upload Form T1322 in My Business Account: Complete Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval) and upload it (along with up to 10 supporting documents in a single session under "Correspondence → Submit documents"). Part 2, Section B of Form T1322 enforces strict word limits: Line 042 (Scientific or technological uncertainty: maximum 500 words), Line 043 (Due diligence completed showing why the existing knowledge base, literature, and experts could not solve the problem: maximum 700 words), and Line 044 (Planned work for the pre-claim approval period of up to 3 years, detailing hypotheses, experiments, and external contractors: maximum 900 words). Section D requires four categories of supporting uploads: (i) project planning documents (Gantt charts, milestones, work breakdown structures), (ii) description of planned internal controls (time-tracking and contemporaneous experimental record protocols), (iii) key supporting technical references (scientific papers, architecture diagrams, patent searches), and (iv) list of project team members with credentials.

Step 3 — Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Within 4 weeks of submitting Form T1322, the CRA assigns an RTA. New SR&ED claimants must attend a mandatory 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting with the RTA (optional or at the RTA's discretion for existing claimants in good standing) to discuss the state of technology, uncertainty, hypothesis, and experimental plan.

Step 4 — Receive Official Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of submitting the completed application, the CRA issues a formal Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If granted, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (provided no material changes are made to the project without notifying the RTA).

body.text: 7.5 Post-Filing Service Standards, FTCAS, Audit Review Procedures, and Dispute Resolution

Once a complete SR&ED claim (Form T661 and Schedule 31 or T2038(IND)) is filed alongside the income tax return, the CRA enforces three published processing service standards for refundable claims (which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time; non-refundable claims have no fixed service standard):

items: 60 Calendar Days: Refundable claims accepted as filed without review.
90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review where all claimed projects were granted Pre-Claim Approval (cutting standard review time in half).
180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for full technical and financial review (including any project not granted pre-claim approval or materially altered from its pre-approved scope).

body.text: First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) and CRA Technical/Financial Reviews

First-time claimants (or businesses that have not filed an SR&ED claim in the preceding 3 years) may be selected for the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS)—a mandatory virtual educational meeting with SR&ED officers that issues a tailored post-meeting advisory report on work identification, expenditure tracking, and documentation protocols without auditing or adjusting the current refund.

For claims selected for technical and financial review via risk assessment or random sampling under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a claim cannot be withdrawn once selected because Form T661 is an integral part of the tax return and the Part 10 certification is irrevocable. Under the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, RTAs and FRs issue an initial letter with a 30-day standard information request timeline and conduct interviews directly with the technical personnel who performed the work. Under subsection 230(1) of the ITA, supporting evidence must be organized and usable; RTAs may reject disorganized paper dumps or unindexed digital drives and issue formal "Better Books and Records" letters requiring signed compliance agreements within 30 days. RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating percentage settlements on eligibility. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a formal Proposal Package containing the RTA's SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and the FR's financial proposal letter, giving the claimant 30 days to submit written representations.
Three-Tier Administrative Dispute Resolution and Judicial Appeals

If a disagreement arises during a review, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns establish a three-step internal escalation path before assessment, followed by three statutory judicial appeal levels after assessment:

items: Administrative Step 1 (RTA and FR): Direct technical and financial dialogue with the assigned reviewers.
Administrative Step 2 (RTM and FRM): Escalation to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Administrative Step 3 (Administrative Review — Form RC532): Before the 30-day proposal window expires and before the file is closed, the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, 13th Floor, Enterprise Building, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review evaluates whether due process was provided and whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation and CRA policy.

Formal Notice of Objection (CRA Appeals Branch — Form T400A / RC592): Within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment, a corporate claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection online via My Business Account or on Form T400A / RC592. (Note: Large corporations with taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000 must specifically quantify the relief sought for each issue and pay 50% of the disputed tax immediately).

Judicial Appeals: If the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the reassessment (or fails to decide within 90 days of the objection), the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada within 90 days of the confirmation notice. Judgments of the Tax Court of Canada may be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal within 30 days (excluding July and August), and further to the Supreme Court of Canada by filing an application for leave to appeal within 60 days (excluding July).

body.text: 8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Case Law and Judicial Audit Precedents

Canadian courts have developed a rigorous body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act. Every technical narrative and audit defence must align with the following controlling precedents:
8.1 Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC)

In Sass Manufacturing, the Tax Court of Canada established the foundational judicial principle distinguishing systematic investigation from unmethodical trial-and-error in shop-floor manufacturing. The Court held that developing a new agricultural axial-flow pump through intuitive adjustments without a structured experimental plan, systematic testing, and recorded measurements of variables did not satisfy the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis".
8.2 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)

Presided over by Justice Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada), Northwest Hydraulic remains the bedrock judicial authority governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada. Evaluating complex physical hydraulic scale modelling of rivers, dams, and spillways, Justice Bowman formulated the Five-Question Test (technological risk or uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses, adherence to the scientific method, technological advancement, and contemporaneous record-keeping as the work progressed) and drew the boundary between technological uncertainty and routine engineering. Justice Bowman held that "routine engineering" encompasses all techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; even if it is uncertain whether a design will achieve its objective until built and tested, if the uncertainty can be resolved by standard engineering procedures without developing new technological knowledge, it is not SR&ED. Conversely, technological uncertainty exists either as system uncertainty (where the behaviour of an integrated system cannot be predicted even though the individual components are well understood) or component uncertainty, and resolving that uncertainty through iterative hypothesis testing constitutes experimental development even if the resulting advancement is incremental.
8.3 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie, the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously elevated Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria to binding appellate law. Dealing with a claimant that developed concrete forming panels and structural durability sensors, Justice Robertson held that repeatability is the essence of the scientific method: while oral testimony from witnesses can establish that work took place, a taxpayer cannot establish that systematic scientific experimentation occurred without objective documentary evidence of the hypotheses formulated, the exact test data generated, and the analytical results.
8.4 C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212, 2002 DTC 2740 (FCA) (aff'g 2000 DTC 674 (TCC))

In C.W. Agencies, the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed Tax Court Justice Bonner's strict definition of a scientific or technological hypothesis in the context of software development. The Courts held that a hypothesis is not merely a commercial goal or a vague statement of intent; rather, a valid SR&ED hypothesis must be a specific, provisional causal proposition capable of being objectively proved or disproved through controlled scientific or technological experimentation.
8.5 Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877 (TCC)

In Data Kinetics, a software company electing the Proxy Method claimed payments made to lease a dedicated telecommunications data line and access a mainframe computer located outside Canada. The CRA disallowed the cost as general overhead covered by the PPA. The Tax Court of Canada reversed the CRA, holding that leasing dedicated bandwidth and mainframe time constituted a lease of tangible optoelectronic and computing equipment (which was not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture). Following Bill C-15's restoration of equipment leases after December 15, 2024, the CRA's Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) expressly incorporates Data Kinetics to allow dedicated bandwidth and remote computing leases under the Proxy Method.
8.6 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6

In Joel Theatrical Rigging, Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed SR&ED claims for two mechanical rigging projects (a motorized hydraulic fire-curtain descent controller and a low-cost manual override mechanism designed to cost $5,000 instead of $25,000). The judgment highlights three critical audit vulnerabilities. First, regarding the absence of qualified technical witnesses, the claimant called only its company president and its external SR&ED tax accountant; no professional engineer (P.Eng.) or technically trained employee who performed the work testified, leading the Court to find that the claimant failed to establish "trained and systematic observation". Second, regarding failure to consult available engineering knowledge, because the claimant never consulted a professional hydraulic engineer, it failed to demonstrate that controlling curtain descent without counterweights or adapting existing $25,000 limit-switch designs could not be solved by routine engineering. Third, regarding vague statements of intent versus testable hypotheses, post-hoc summaries stating "next steps: experiment with hydraulic pumps and valves" or visually watching dropped weights without recording exact weights and descent times were held to be informal trial-and-error, not scientific hypothesis testing.
8.7 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)

In both Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88, involving metal stamping tooling) and National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72, written by Justice Rennie involving software consulting), taxpayers challenged the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion directly before the Federal Court of Appeal, arguing that because the phrase "scientific method" does not appear verbatim in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the Tax Court erred in requiring adherence to the scientific method. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected this argument in both appeals, holding that the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test—including methodical adherence to the scientific method (formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses through systematic observation and measurement)—is the settled, mandatory legal interpretation of "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis" in subsection 248(1). In National R&D, the Federal Court of Appeal also upheld the rejection of vague, post-hoc technical reconstructions that lacked a logical progression between experimental premise and observed result.
8.8 Canafric Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2023 TCC 108

In Canafric, a frozen pie manufacturer appealed the CRA's denial of seven SR&ED projects (2013–2016) aimed at formulating preservative-free frozen meat pies with extended shelf life and reduced sodium and fat without crust degradation. During the review, the CRA's RTA dismissively stated: "A pie is a pie, what is the big deal about it." Chief Justice Rossiter allowed the taxpayer's appeal in full, holding that all seven projects qualified as SR&ED. Citing the Federal Court of Appeal's observation in National R&D that statutory criteria must be applied with "amplitude and precision... as required by the circumstances of the case," Chief Justice Rossiter established that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria must be applied in a context-sensitive, industry-appropriate manner rather than as a rigid laboratory straitjacket against non-traditional manufacturing sectors. Because Canafric systematically formulated ingredient-interaction hypotheses, tested numbered experimental batches, and recorded microbial and organoleptic test results, it satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic questions.
8.9 Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 103 (aff'd FCA), and CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178 (SCC Leave Refused 2023)

In Immunovaccine (2013 TCC 103, involving $3,786,474 in conditionally repayable ACOA funding) and CAE Inc. (2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 178, involving $250,000,000 in unconditionally repayable 2.5% interest loans from Industry Canada), the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal held that government funding—even when structured as an unconditionally repayable loan—constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) unless the funding was advanced on "ordinary commercial agreement" terms motivated by the ordinary commercial return of a lender. As detailed in Section 5.8, while Immunovaccine continues to govern forgivable or conditionally royalty-repayable grants and contributions, the result of CAE Inc. on unconditionally repayable below-market government debt was legislatively overturned retroactive to January 1, 2020, by Bill C-69 (2024) through the enactment of the "excluded loan" carve-out in subsection 12(11), subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix), and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act.
